app.title: GeoLatido
app.tagline: What changed, what was not detected and what cannot be known, with the data behind it.

public.question: What did the radar see in this area?
public.lead: NISAR is a radar satellite from the space agencies of the United States (NASA) and India (ISRO). It sees through clouds and passes over each area every 12 days. Here you can see what it noticed between two passes, what it could not see and what is still unknown.

states.label: How to read each answer
states.change_probable: The radar signal changed more than its noise over enough ground. It does not say why.
states.no_detectable_change: The area could be observed and no change larger than the noise was seen.
states.not_observable: The radar could not see it, and the reason is given.

evidence.heading: Evidence
evidence.ruleValue: Probable change from {{change}} of the observed area; not observable if less than {{observed}} is observed.
evidence.json: View this verdict's JSON in the API

explain.changed: Share of what the radar could see where the signal changed more than the threshold.
explain.observed: Share of the area the radar could see well on both dates.
explain.rule: The system sets these limits and states them; the person asking does not choose them.
explain.threshold: The decibel (dB) measures the signal returning to the radar: 3 dB is double or half. HH and HV are two polarizations: HH responds more to smooth water and buildings, HV to vegetation.
explain.meanChange: Average change over the whole observed area. Negative: the signal went down.
explain.sceneShift: If the whole scene goes up or down at once (for example, with wet soil), that general change is not local.

story.heading: The story of Parral in three scenes
story.intro: Three questions about Hidalgo del Parral. Each answer comes from the API with the already processed data, with what is known and what is not.
story.error: This scene could not be loaded. The others are still available.

storm.title: 1. The storm of 1 July 2026
storm.text: On 1 July 2026, a storm left water in the streets of Parral and swept a vehicle along the Arroyo de las Quintas. Chihuahua Civil Protection recorded 22.8 mm of rain in one hour. Did the satellite pass during the time we assume it lasted?
storm.source: Source: bulletin of the State Civil Protection Coordination, Government of Chihuahua (1 July 2026)

monsoon.title: 2. A date pair in August
monsoon.text: From 16 to 28 August 2026. This is what the radar says about that date pair, and what it cannot prove.
monsoon.showOnMap: Show this pair on the map

mine.title: 3. A point next to the La Prieta Mine
mine.text: We took a point next to the La Prieta Mine, according to OpenStreetMap, and looked at what the radar detected in each date pair.
mine.count: {{same}} of {{total}} pairs with no detectable change at this point.
mine.note: Detecting no change is also information, but it does not prove that nothing changed: it says the radar saw no change larger than its threshold.

event.heading: Could the satellite see an event?
event.intro: Tell us when something happened (a storm, a river flood, a wildfire) and we will tell you whether NISAR passed over the area during the time we assume it lasted. It does not say whether anything changed.
event.dateHelp: Dates and times are in UTC (universal time). If it is already evening in the area, in UTC it may be the next day.
event.timeHelp: Convert local time to UTC with the area's offset; for example, in Chihuahua UTC is local time plus 6 hours.
event.error: The check could not be done. Review the date and try again.

state.observable: Observable: a pass fell within the event's assumed duration

event.observableNote: This does not say that anything changed: for that, look at the verdict for the date pair that includes that pass.

online.heading: Verdicts for this area
online.series: Series {{id}} ({{pol}}): its {{dates}} most recent dates are processed.
online.noSeries: NISAR has no series with HH and HV here (or fewer than two dates), and change detection needs both polarizations. You can still see the passes:

state.queued: Queued: one area is processed at a time.
state.running: Reading only the area from NASA in memory (no subsets stored), several dates at once, computing as they arrive. A 0.3° area takes about 2 to 3 minutes, depending on the connection.
state.done: Done: the area now has verdicts.

welcome.title: Welcome to GeoLatido
welcome.text: GeoLatido listens to the heartbeat of the Earth's surface with the NASA–ISRO NISAR radar: what changed, what was not detected and what cannot be known, anywhere in the world. Search for a city above or click on the map to start.
welcome.noAccount: You do not need an account: everything looks the same without signing in. An account is only for publishing and rating stories.
